blocks.text: Is the Bondi Hum real or a hoax? Here's my honest answer after years of fielding this question over coffee on the promenade: it's real in the sense that people genuinely hear it — it isn't invented for attention — but nobody has ever pinned down a confirmed external source, and a good chunk of the science now points inward rather than out to sea. So not a hoax, but not the tidy villain (a secret pump, a rogue transformer) that everyone hopes to catch either.

items.label: Who hears it
items.value: A small minority, roughly 2–4% in affected areas

blocks.text: So what exactly is the Bondi Hum?

People who hear it describe a steady, monotonous drone — like a distant idling truck, a far-off industrial fan, or a low-flying plane that never arrives. It's low-frequency, it's relentless, and here's the strange part: the person next to you often can't hear a thing. It tends to be loudest indoors and after dark, when the general clamour of a busy beachside suburb dies down and there's nothing to mask it.

For most of us it's a curiosity. For the unlucky few who genuinely perceive it, it can be miserable — disturbed sleep, headaches, a sense of pressure or vibration, and the particular frustration of a problem that no one else can hear and no meter has definitively caught.

The thing I always tell people is that Bondi isn't special here. "The Hum" is a global phenomenon reported for decades. It surfaced famously in Bristol, England, in the mid-1970s, then in the 1990s in places like Taos, New Mexico and Kokomo, Indiana — each with its own name and its own baffled residents. The reports are remarkably consistent: a low rumble, usually described in the 30–80 Hz range, worse at night, and audible to only a small slice of the local population.

If you think you're hearing it, try a simple test: step well away from the building and see whether it fades. A true external low-frequency source usually changes as you move; a hum that follows you everywhere, even outdoors in the open, is a strong hint the source may be your own hearing system rather than the neighbourhood.
Real or hoax? Where the science actually sits

This is where it gets interesting. A 2026 study led by Professor Markus Drexl and colleagues at Norway's NTNU tested people who hear the Hum and found that, for most of them, the likeliest explanation is low-frequency tinnitus — a sound generated within the auditory system itself, even though it feels utterly external. Of 28 participants, only two showed better-than-average low-frequency hearing, and none produced the tell-tale emissions you'd expect if their ears were unusually sensitive. In other words, most of the time the hum may be coming from inside the listener, not the coastline.

That said, the researchers were careful — and so am I. They didn't rule external sources out entirely, and standard hearing tests can miss extremely narrow sensitivities. Some hums genuinely are real machinery: the Bristol case and others have at times been traced to industrial or infrastructure noise. So the honest verdict is a split one. Not a hoax; partly a real acoustic quirk of hearing; occasionally a real external source that simply hasn't been found.

blocks.title: If it's affecting your health
blocks.text: A hum that's wrecking your sleep or causing headaches and stress is worth taking seriously. See a GP or an audiologist — low-frequency tinnitus is a recognised, manageable condition, and ruling it in or out is far more useful than chasing a phantom machine. If you're convinced it's an external source, the NSW EPA is the body that handles noise complaints.
What locals and authorities have made of it

Over the years, eastern-suburbs residents have raised low-frequency noise with local authorities, and the usual suspects — nearby traffic, sewerage infrastructure, industrial plant — have been floated and largely dismissed without a smoking gun. The NSW Environment Protection Authority is the agency that investigates persistent noise complaints across Sydney, and their published noise-investigation updates are the best place to check whether anything current is on their radar. For the Bondi Hum specifically, no conclusive cause has ever been confirmed.

items.q: Is the Bondi Hum a hoax?
items.a: No. People genuinely perceive it — it isn't made up. What's unproven is the cause. There's no confirmed external source, and recent research suggests that for many hearers it may be a form of low-frequency tinnitus generated within the ear itself.

items.q: Why can only some people hear the Bondi Hum?
items.a: That's the defining feature of 'the Hum' everywhere: only a small minority — very roughly 2–4% in affected areas — report it. If it were loud environmental noise, most people nearby would notice it, which is part of why an internal, hearing-based explanation is taken seriously.

items.q: Has the cause of the Bondi Hum ever been found?
items.a: No. Suggested sources like traffic, sewerage plant and industrial equipment have been considered and not confirmed. As with the Taos and Bristol hums, no definitive external cause has been established for Bondi.

items.q: What should I do if I can hear it?
items.a: Try moving well away from any building to see if it fades. If it persists and affects your sleep or wellbeing, see a GP or audiologist about low-frequency tinnitus. If you believe it's genuinely an outside source, the NSW EPA handles noise investigations.

blocks.text: So, real or hoax? Neither label quite fits, and that's exactly why the Bondi Hum has stuck around in local folklore. It sits in the genuinely unexplained middle — a real experience with a stubbornly elusive cause. Next time someone swears blind they can hear a droning out over the water on a still night, don't dismiss them. They might just be one of the few. And if you're one too, you're in surprisingly good company, all the way from Taos to Bristol.
